title: This Artist Types Pictures Instead of Drawing Them
summary: What if you could make a picture without drawing a single line? James Cook does it with a typewriter. He's a 29-year-old artist from London who creates amazing pictures using only the keys on old-fashioned typewriters. He has over 100 of them! Cook first saw typewriter art in high school. He learned about Paul Smith, an artist with cerebral palsy who couldn't hold a pen, so he used a typewriter instead. Cook tried it and was hooked. Now he makes cityscapes of London and Tokyo, and portraits of famous artists like Frida Kahlo. One of his coolest pieces is a drawing of Wimbledon's Centre Court, the famous tennis court. It took four weeks and more than one million keystrokes to finish! He uses capital 'E's for buildings and windows, and the '@' symbol for shadows. He presses the keys harder or softer to make things look light or dark. Each artwork takes a week to three months. He sells them for $4,000 to $40,000. But you can buy a print for around $110. Cook says the limits of the typewriter are what make it fun. 'You have to work with a fixed set of tools,' he says. 'That forces you to think differently.'
why_it_matters: It reminds you that you don't need fancy new tools to be creative — you can make something cool with whatever is already in front of you.

background_read: Before computers, people wrote letters and reports on typewriters — machines with a keyboard that stamps one letter at a time onto paper.

Paul Smith was a real American artist who was born with cerebral palsy (a condition that makes it hard to control your muscles), and because holding a pen was very hard for him, he typed pictures on a typewriter instead.
Wimbledon's Centre Court is the main grass court at the world's oldest tennis tournament, held every year in London, and it is one of the most famous sports arenas on Earth.
Article_Structure: WHO: James Cook, a 29-year-old artist from London who types pictures instead of drawing them.
WHAT: He makes cityscapes and portraits on old typewriters, using letters and symbols like 'E' and '@' instead of paint.
WHERE: In London — he lives there and makes cityscapes of London and Tokyo, and one piece shows Wimbledon's Centre Court.
WHY: He says the typewriter's limits make the art fun, because a fixed set of tools forces him to think differently.

perspectives.description: They think typed pictures are amazing because it is so hard to build a whole scene out of letters and symbols.

perspectives.perspective: People who might buy the art
perspectives.description: Some may think $4,000 is a lot for a picture made of letters, while others say it is fair because each one takes weeks of work — and prints cost much less.
They can see that an old machine can be as good as new paints, which means you don't need expensive supplies to make something special.
